overview: This card concerns Western Sahara, its Sahrawi people and an unresolved decolonization dispute; it does not endorse Morocco’s sovereignty claim or the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic’s claim. The atlas begins around 1945 and repeatedly draws the entire territory as one polygon. That shape hides the military berm, different zones of de facto administration and operation, minefields and refugee camps near Tindouf in Algeria. A January 2026 UN paper still described competing Moroccan and Frente POLISARIO positions, low-intensity hostilities and an unfinished political process. The SADR alias is therefore a search aid, not a neutral one-to-one identity. Neither atlas boundaries nor present control settles legal title or the people’s right to self-determination.

periods.title: Spanish colonial rule
periods.summary: Spain colonized the territory it called Spanish Sahara; the atlas joins the story only around 1945.

periods.title: A UN-listed decolonization case
periods.summary: The United Nations listed Spanish Sahara as a Non-Self-Governing Territory in 1963, while demands for self-determination grew.

periods.title: Spanish withdrawal, competing claims and war
periods.summary: Spain withdrew after the Madrid Agreement; Morocco and Mauritania took administrative control in areas, Polisario proclaimed the SADR, and war followed.

periods.title: War after Mauritania’s withdrawal
periods.summary: Mauritania withdrew in 1979; fighting between Morocco and Frente POLISARIO continued until settlement proposals and a ceasefire took effect in 1991.

periods.title: Ceasefire and an unheld referendum
periods.summary: A UN-backed ceasefire and MINURSO mission began in 1991, but the planned act of self-determination was not completed.

periods.title: Ceasefire breakdown and low-intensity hostilities
periods.summary: The ceasefire broke down in 2020; MINURSO remained while reported fire and strikes continued around and across the berm.

periods.title: Renewed UN talks without a settled status
periods.summary: Resolution 2797 extended MINURSO through October 2026 and made Morocco’s autonomy proposal the basis for talks while retaining self-determination and mutual agreement as requirements.

sections.title: What is settled, what is claimed and what is controlled

items.text: Western Sahara has remained on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories since 1963. Spain told the UN that it ended its presence in February 1976, and the UN status page lists no current administering Power. Those facts leave decolonization unresolved. Calling the whole atlas polygon “Morocco,” “SADR” or an independent state as if no dispute existed would turn a legal and political question into a misleading map label.

The International Court of Justice found in 1975 that Western Sahara was not terra nullius when Spain colonized it: peoples lived there in socially and politically organized tribes. The Court found some ties of allegiance to Morocco’s sultan and land-use ties with a Mauritanian entity, but no territorial-sovereignty tie capable of displacing self-determination through the free and genuine will of the territory’s people.

The 1975 Madrid Agreement did not transfer sovereignty to Morocco or Mauritania and did not make either a UN administering Power, the UN Legal Counsel concluded in 2002. Morocco has nevertheless administered the territory after Mauritania’s 1979 withdrawal, without appearing as administering Power on the UN list. De facto administration, a sovereignty claim and internationally settled title are three different things.

The 2026 UN working paper describes Moroccan authorities carrying out censuses and development west of the berm, while MINURSO deals separately with Frente POLISARIO and operations east of it. Morocco advances sovereignty and autonomy; Polisario advances self-determination and independence. These attributed positions and areas of effective activity explain the divided reality. They do not convert the berm into an international border or settle ownership of either side.

Frente POLISARIO proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic in 1976. The African Union lists the Sahrawi Republic as a member since 22 February 1982. That is important institutional recognition, but it is not universal recognition and does not mean the SADR effectively administers every point inside the atlas polygon. The UN continues to handle Western Sahara as a separate decolonization question.

A written Arabic sample is الصحراء الغربية, al-Sahra al-Gharbiyya, meaning “Western Sahara.” This is the UN’s Arabic geographical term, written from right to left in Modern Standard Arabic. Hassaniya, an Arabic variety widely spoken in Western Sahara and Mauritania, is central to many Sahrawi conversations. The sample is therefore an official place-name, not an invented Hassaniya sentence and not a sovereignty ruling.

MINURSO began in 1991 to support settlement proposals and a ceasefire. The referendum in its name has not occurred, and the ceasefire broke down in 2020. The mission now monitors, investigates and reports while trying to reduce tensions. A peacekeeping mission can limit danger without solving the political question that caused it; “still present” and “mission accomplished” are very different descriptions.

Between July 2024 and June 2025, MINURSO mine-action teams released 1,385,558 square metres of land and found and destroyed 335 items of explosive ordnance. They also supported route checks and risk education. That is measurable safety work, but it does not mean Western Sahara is cleared: mines and unexploded weapons still shape movement, livelihoods and UN operations.

Security Council resolution 2797, adopted in October 2025, extended MINURSO to 31 October 2026. It directed negotiations to use Morocco’s autonomy proposal as a basis and said genuine autonomy could be a feasible outcome, while still requiring a mutually acceptable solution providing self-determination. This changed the Council’s negotiating language; it did not record a final agreement or settle title by itself.

Sahrawi refugee education in the five camps near Tindouf is community-based and operated by refugees. UNICEF reported 40,050 children aged three to sixteen in 89 schools and care centres in 2023; 82 per cent of the 1,800 education workers were women. Passing rates and minimum-competency results also showed serious gaps. Running a school system in exile is an achievement, while needing aid and better learning outcomes remains a limitation.

sections.title: Tents, tea, cameras and family learning

items.text: One UNHCR profile follows a grandmother whose family used both a mud-brick house and a traditional tent. The tent was a place to sleep, eat, drink tea and welcome guests, and older women worried that younger people had fewer chances to learn tent weaving and repair. A tent can be architecture, hospitality and a portable family memory, but one household cannot represent every Sahrawi home.

In September 2025, twenty Sahrawi refugee children from all five camps joined a photography workshop; for many it was their first time holding a camera. They chose what to photograph and wrote their own captions about daily life and dreams. Nine-year-old Cherifa wanted to become a lawyer. The project was small, but it let children become the authors rather than only the subjects of a refugee story.

A UNHCR profile of a Sahrawi graduate describes a multilingual life spanning camp school, study elsewhere and teaching back in the camps. He spoke Hassaniya, Arabic, English, Spanish and German, yet struggled to find paid work matching his education. His experience shows how language learning can connect worlds while protracted displacement closes ordinary career doors. It is one person’s path, not a claim that everyone speaks five languages.

Older students often leave their families to attend secondary or higher education in Algeria, while camp schools depend heavily on refugee teachers. UNICEF also supports school supplies, inclusive centres and teacher training. Education can therefore mean a morning walk to a local classroom, boarding far away, or learning in a disability-support centre. Family separation for study is an opportunity and a cost, not a simple success statistic.

sections.title: Midwives, water trucks and the unglamorous work of toilets

items.text: Sahrawi midwives and community health workers monitor pregnancy, newborns, immunization, nutrition and referrals in the refugee camps, with UNICEF supporting training and maternal-child care. Community medicine is strongest when a trained neighbour can spot danger early, but local skill cannot substitute for medicines, staff and reliable funding.

The inter-agency report published in May 2025 recorded measles, whooping cough, chickenpox and hepatitis A outbreaks during 2024. Vaccination coverage had improved, but the camp health system still faced shortages of staff, medicines and operating support. Dates matter here: this is evidence about one reporting year, not a claim that every outbreak continued unchanged through 2026.

Water in the camps arrives through both pipes and trucks. The 2024-2025 response plan said that in 2022 only Dakhla camp met the UNHCR benchmark of twenty litres per person per day; the other camps did not. Planned work included extending networks and maintaining systems. A water truck is essential infrastructure on wheels, but families should not have to plan every cup around its arrival.

The same response plan treats toilets, waste collection and handwashing as connected public-health systems. It called for WASH facilities in schools and clinics, household waste collection, maintained landfill areas and hygiene supplies, especially for women. A plastic-recycling project begun in 2021 tried to turn some discarded material into saleable products. The plan records needs and intended work, not proof that every toilet or tap was already functioning.

ending.text: Western Sahara has no agreed political ending. The January 2026 UN paper still described competing parties, low-intensity hostilities and unresolved negotiations; resolution 2797 kept MINURSO authorized through 31 October 2026. The atlas’s 2100 endpoint is only a software interval, not a prediction that one claim will win or that the dispute will last that long.
